Among the 318 RATIFY patients aged 18-60 with FLT3-ITD AML for whom complete 2017 ELN genetic risk categorization using NPM1/FLT3-ITD status together with RUNX1, ASXL1, TP53 and cytogenetic risk features was possible, 5-year overall survival was 0.62 for favorable risk, 0.43 for intermediate risk, and 0.33 for adverse risk; the ELN classification remained a significant prognostic variable in multivariable analysis.

cards.interpretation: CHIP is defined by a somatic mutation in a myeloid malignancy-associated gene detected in blood or marrow at VAF ≥2% (≥4% for X-linked mutations in males), in a person without a diagnosed haematologic disorder or unexplained cytopenia.
CCUS is CHIP accompanied by one or more persistent otherwise-unexplained cytopenias that do not meet diagnostic criteria for a defined myeloid neoplasm.
For CCUS, MDS and MDS/MPN, cytopenia thresholds are haemoglobin <13 g/dL in males or <12 g/dL in females, ANC <1.8 ×10^9/L, and platelets <150 ×10^9/L.
CML is defined by the BCR::ABL1 fusion resulting from t(9;22)(q34;q11).
In CML, ABL1 kinase mutations are described as a source of TKI resistance and a key disease attribute in the current classification.
CML blast phase is defined by ≥20% myeloid blasts in blood or marrow, extramedullary blast proliferation, or increased lymphoblasts in blood or marrow; accelerated phase is omitted from WHO5.
Major PV diagnostic criteria include elevated haemoglobin and/or haematocrit, marrow panmyelosis with pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes, and JAK2 p.V617F or a JAK2 exon 12 mutation.
In PMF, mutations in EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SRSF2, U2AF1 and ASXL1 are associated with poorer prognostic risk.
CNL is a BCR::ABL1-negative MPN characterized by sustained neutrophilia with WBC ≥25 ×10^9/L and ≥80% segmented neutrophils/bands, neutrophilic marrow hypercellularity and hepatosplenomegaly.
CEL is characterized by sustained clonal proliferation of morphologically abnormal eosinophils/eosinophil precursors causing persistent blood and marrow hypereosinophilia.
For CEL, the interval required to define sustained hypereosinophilia is 4 weeks rather than 6 months.
CEL requires both evidence of clonality and abnormal bone-marrow morphology, such as megakaryocytic or erythroid dysplasia.
For CEL, increased blasts (≥2% in blood or 5–19% in marrow) are no longer an alternative to demonstrating clonality.
Updated JMML criteria require exclusion of KMT2A rearrangements.
JMML diagnosis emphasizes molecular studies demonstrating RAS-pathway activation together with clinical and laboratory criteria.
JMML initiated by somatic PTPN11 mutations is among the most aggressive genetic types.
A subset of JMML is associated with pathogenic germline CBL variants.
JMML associated with pathogenic germline CBL variants can occasionally undergo spontaneous remission.
In systemic mastocytosis, KIT p.D816V with VAF ≥10% in bone-marrow cells or peripheral-blood leukocytes qualifies as a B-finding.
Any KIT mutation causing ligand-independent activation is accepted as a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis.
Well-differentiated systemic mastocytosis may occur in any systemic-mastocytosis subtype; most cases lack KIT codon 816 mutation and typically show CD25/CD2 negativity with CD30 positivity.
MDS is defined by cytopenias and morphologic dysplasia, with a recommended dysplasia threshold of 10% for all lineages.
Within genetically defined MDS, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation supersedes MDS-5q and MDS-SF3B1 in the WHO5 hierarchy.
In MDS-5q, an SF3B1 mutation or a TP53 mutation that is not multi-hit does not by itself override the MDS-5q diagnosis.
For SF3B1-wild-type MDS with ≥15% ring sideroblasts, “MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts” remains an acceptable alternative designation.

Clinical assessment of biallelic TP53 alterations in MDS uses sequencing covering at least exons 4–11 together with copy-number assessment; TP53 locus loss may also be inferred by next-generation sequencing.
In MDS, TP53 VAF ≥50% may be regarded as presumptive, but not definitive, evidence of trans-allelic copy loss or copy-neutral LOH when a constitutional TP53 variant has been ruled out.
When two or more TP53 mutations are detected in MDS, they usually affect both alleles and may be considered multi-hit status.
MDS with biallelic TP53 alterations is regarded as very high risk in IPSS-R and is usually associated with complex or very complex karyotype.
Published data support considering MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation as AML-equivalent for therapeutic purposes.
Pathogenic germline GATA2 or DDX41 variants can present with hypoplastic marrow and evolve to MDS and/or AML.
In the hypoplastic-marrow differential, individuals with germline GATA2 or DDX41 pathogenic variants are described as not responding to immunosuppressive treatment.
WHO5 retains a 20% blast cutoff to delineate MDS from AML while removing blast cutoffs for most AML types with defining genetic abnormalities.
MDS-IB2 may be regarded as AML-equivalent for therapeutic considerations and, when appropriate, clinical-trial design.

In childhood MDS with low blasts, monosomy 7, 7q deletion, or complex karyotype is associated with increased risk of AML progression and is typically treated with haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
CMML requires persistent absolute peripheral-blood monocytosis ≥0.5 ×10^9/L and relative monocytosis ≥10%.
When absolute monocytosis is ≥0.5 but <1.0 ×10^9/L, CMML diagnosis requires a clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality and dysplasia in at least one lineage.
In a patient with monocytosis, a documented MPN history excludes CMML; marrow MPN features and/or a high burden of JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations supports MPN with monocytosis rather than CMML.

In a suspected CMML case with eosinophilia, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine-kinase gene fusions should be excluded by assessing for PDGFRA rearrangement (most commonly FIP1L1::PDGFRA), PDGFRB rearrangement (most commonly ETV6::PDGFRB), FGFR1 rearrangement, JAK2 rearrangement, FLT3 rearrangement, ETV6::ABL1, and other defined tyrosine-kinase fusions including ETV6::FGFR2, ETV6::LYN, ETV6::NTRK3, RANBP2::ALK, BCR::RET, and FGFR1OP::RET. WHO5 treats PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2 and FLT3 as rearrangement-defined categories rather than restricting them to a single fusion partner.

cards.interpretation: MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis is redefined on the basis of SF3B1 mutation and renamed MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis.

WHO5 recognizes AML with PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1 and CBFB::MYH11 as AML types with defining genetic abnormalities.
AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation are the defining-genetic-abnormality AML types that still require at least 20% blasts; for BCR::ABL1 this avoids overlap with CML.
AML with KMT2A, MECOM or NUP98 rearrangement may be diagnosed with a blast count below 20%.
KMT2A, MECOM and NUP98 rearrangements, particularly NUP98 rearrangements, may be cryptic on conventional karyotyping.
For KMT2A-rearranged AML, identifying the fusion partner is desirable because it can provide prognostic information.
For KMT2A-rearranged AML, identifying the fusion partner is desirable because it may affect disease monitoring.
AML with NPM1 mutation can be diagnosed irrespective of blast count, with clinicopathologic correlation.
MDS or MDS/MPN cases with NPM1 mutation are reported to progress to AML in a short period.
AML with CEBPA mutation includes biallelic CEBPA mutations and single CEBPA mutations in the basic leucine zipper region.
A single CEBPA mutation in the bZIP region is associated with favourable prognosis in children and adults up to age 70.
Somatic RUNX1 mutation is not sufficient to define a standalone WHO5 AML type because it lacks specificity across defining molecular contexts.
AML, myelodysplasia-related has a mutation-based definition that includes SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, ASXL1, EZH2, BCOR or STAG2.
Morphologic myelodysplasia alone is no longer sufficient to diagnose AML, myelodysplasia-related.
In acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia, the RAM immunophenotype correlates with CBFA2T3::GLIS2, a subtype of AML with other defined genetic alterations.
KIT mutations remain relevant prognostic factors in the genetically defined AML context discussed by WHO5.
WHO5 emphasizes the increased importance of highly sensitive MRD evaluation techniques in the genetically defined AML context of PML::RARA and RUNX1::RUNX1T1.
Post-induction MRD status is a prognostic factor in the genetically defined AML context discussed for PML::RARA and RUNX1::RUNX1T1 AML.

In AML or MDS after cytotoxic therapy, outcomes are generally worse with biallelic/multi-hit TP53 alterations, including ≥2 TP53 mutations or a TP53 mutation with 17p/TP53 deletion or copy-neutral LOH.
In myeloid neoplasms after cytotoxic therapy, PPM1D and other DNA-damage-response gene mutations may warrant additional work-up for germline predisposition.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic CEBPA variant is recognized as CEBPA-associated familial AML within myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic DDX41 variant is a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition subtype.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic TP53 variant (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) is a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition subtype.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic RUNX1 variant defines familial platelet disorder with associated myeloid malignancy.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic ANKRD26 variant (Thrombocytopenia 2) is recognized among myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and a pre-existing platelet disorder.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic ETV6 variant (Thrombocytopenia 5) is recognized among myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and a pre-existing platelet disorder.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic GATA2 variant (GATA2 deficiency) is recognized among myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and potential organ dysfunction.
CBL syndrome is included among RASopathies associated with myeloid-neoplasm germline predisposition.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic SAMD9 variant (MIRAGE syndrome) is a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition state.
A germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic SAMD9L variant is recognized in SAMD9L-related ataxia-pancytopenia syndrome; ataxia is not always present.
Biallelic germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic BLM variants (Bloom syndrome) are a recognized myeloid-neoplasm predisposition state.
Before a diagnosis of CEL is rendered, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine-kinase gene fusions must be excluded.
For MLN-TK with PDGFRA or PDGFRB rearrangement, TKI therapy—particularly imatinib—has dramatically altered the natural history.
MLN-TK with FGFR1, JAK2 or FLT3 fusions or ETV6::ABL1 has more variable sensitivity to available newer-generation TKIs.
For MLN-TK with FGFR1, JAK2 or FLT3 fusions or ETV6::ABL1, long-term disease-free survival may in most cases require allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
WHO5 lists mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia with BCR::ABL1 fusion and with KMT2A rearrangement among acute leukaemias of ambiguous lineage with defining genetic abnormalities.
MPAL with ZNF384 rearrangement is a WHO5 subtype of acute leukaemia with a defining genetic alteration and commonly has a B/myeloid immunophenotype.
Acute leukaemia of ambiguous lineage with BCL11B rearrangement is a WHO5 subtype with a defining genetic alteration and may occur with heterogeneous immunophenotypes.
For flow-cytometric MPO assessment in acute leukaemia, a >10% positivity threshold appears to improve specificity over 3%, but WHO5 states that no consensus cutoff has been established.
BPDCN immunophenotypic diagnosis requires either CD123 plus one other pDC marker with CD4 and/or CD56, or any three pDC markers with absence of all expected negative markers.

cards.interpretation: In CML, major-route additional clonal cytogenetic abnormalities present at diagnosis or acquired during treatment are a hallmark of accelerated phase.
CML accelerated phase is defined by 10%-19% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow.
CML blast phase is defined by at least 20% blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow.
JAK2 V617F/exon 12, CALR, and MPL driver mutations support the diagnosis of PV, ET, or PMF and help distinguish driver-positive from triple-negative disease.
For PV, ET, and PMF driver testing, the ICC recommends highly sensitive single-target or multigene assays with approximately 1% VAF sensitivity.
A JAK2 V617F VAF below 1% should prompt a search for coexisting canonical CALR and MPL mutations.
In suspected triple-negative ET or PMF, searching for noncanonical JAK2 and MPL mutations is encouraged.
In PV, JAK2 exon 12-mutated disease is reported to have prognosis similar to JAK2 V617F-mutated disease.
In JAK2 exon 12-mutated PV with isolated erythrocytosis and erythroid-predominant marrow, panmyelosis may not be an applicable diagnostic criterion.
JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation is a major diagnostic criterion for essential thrombocythemia.
JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation is a major diagnostic criterion for polycythemia vera.
In PV with sustained absolute erythrocytosis at the stated high hemoglobin/hematocrit thresholds, bone marrow biopsy may not be required when JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation is present.
JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation is a major molecular diagnostic criterion for prefibrotic or overt primary myelofibrosis.
Mutations in ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 can support the clonal nature of suspected PMF.
In PMF with monocytosis, a higher VAF of an MPN-associated driver mutation supports PMF with monocytosis rather than CMML.
Activating CSF3R driver mutations are the diagnostic genetic signature of CNL.
Absence of a CSF3R mutation does not exclude CNL.
CSF3R T618I or another activating CSF3R mutation satisfies the molecular diagnostic criterion for CNL.
CNL requires exclusion of BCR::ABL1-positive CML and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase fusions.
For CNL with CSF3R T618I or another activating CSF3R mutation, the leukocytosis threshold is at least 13 × 10^9/L; without an activating CSF3R mutation, the threshold is at least 25 × 10^9/L.
CNL with 10%-19% blasts in blood or bone marrow is classified as accelerated phase.
CNL with at least 20% blasts in blood or bone marrow is classified as blast phase.
CEL, NOS requires absence of BCR::ABL1, other ABL1, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, or FLT3 tyrosine-kinase fusions.
JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation satisfies the molecular clonality criterion for MPN-U.
Mutations such as ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 support the clonal nature of MPN-U.

KIT D816V or another activating KIT mutation in marrow, blood, or another extracutaneous organ is a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis.
High-sensitivity PCR is recommended for KIT D816V testing in suspected systemic mastocytosis to reduce false-negative results.
If KIT D816V testing is negative in suspected systemic mastocytosis, exclusion of other KIT mutation variants is strongly recommended.
Identification of a tyrosine-kinase fusion associated with M/LN-eo excludes a diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis.
In suspected systemic mastocytosis without a KIT mutation, particularly with eosinophilia, M/LN-eo-associated tyrosine-kinase fusions should be excluded.
Rare well-differentiated systemic mastocytosis cases that typically lack KIT D816V may have a higher response rate to conventional tyrosine-kinase inhibitors.

In systemic mastocytosis, high KIT D816V VAF, particularly with monocytosis, eosinophilia, splenomegaly, elevated LDH, or additional myeloid mutations, raises suspicion for an associated myeloid neoplasm.
In CMML, common myeloid mutations including SRSF2, TET2, ASXL1, SETBP1, NRAS, KRAS, RUNX1, CBL, and EZH2 can provide molecular evidence of clonality.
ASXL1 mutations in CMML have prognostic implications.
NPM1 mutation in CMML is associated with a particularly aggressive clinical course and rapid progression to acute leukemia.
Development of an NPM1 mutation in established CMML should be noted but does not by itself define de novo AML.
When clonality is established, CMML can be diagnosed with an absolute monocyte count of at least 0.5 × 10^9/L provided monocytes remain at least 10% of WBC.
The myeloproliferative subtype of CMML is defined by WBC greater than 13 × 10^9/L.
In aCML, absence of JAK2, CALR, and MPL driver mutations supports the diagnosis, whereas an MPN history or these driver mutations tends to exclude aCML.
SETBP1 mutation, often with ASXL1 co-mutation, supports a diagnosis of aCML.
CSF3R mutation is uncommon in aCML and, if detected, should prompt morphologic review to exclude CNL.
aCML requires absence of BCR::ABL1.
aCML requires absence of genetic abnormalities defining myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase fusions.
MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis requires an SF3B1 mutation with VAF greater than 10%.
When the qualifying SF3B1 mutation is present in MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis, ring sideroblasts are not required for diagnosis.
In MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis, JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL W515 co-mutation is not required but supports the diagnosis.
MDS-SF3B1 that later develops thrombocytosis is classified as thrombocytotic progression of MDS-SF3B1 rather than as MDS/MPN.
MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis requires absence of BCR::ABL1.
MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis requires absence of genetic abnormalities defining myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase fusions.
For MDS/MPN, NOS, an MPN history or JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation—particularly at high VAF—tends to exclude the diagnosis.

cards.interpretation: A somatic mutation in PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, or RRAS is a qualifying genetic route for JMML.

Germline CBL mutation with acquired loss of heterozygosity is a qualifying genetic route for JMML.
JMML associated with NF1 involves a germline NF1 event that progresses to malignancy through acquired biallelic inactivation in hematopoietic cells.
JMML associated with CBL involves a germline CBL event that usually progresses to malignancy through acquired biallelic inactivation in hematopoietic cells.
PTPN11-, NRAS-, and KRAS-mutated JMML are characterized by heterozygous somatic gain-of-function mutations in children without germline disease.
Germline PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, or RIT1 mutations in Noonan syndrome can cause a transient myeloproliferative disorder in the first year of life.
Germline CEBPA predisposes to AML.
Germline DDX41 predisposes to both myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms.
Germline TP53 in Li-Fraumeni syndrome predisposes to myeloid and lymphoid malignancies in both treatment-naive and therapy-related settings.
Germline RUNX1 predisposition is associated with a constitutional platelet disorder and can predispose to myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms.

Germline ETV6 predisposition is associated with a constitutional platelet disorder and can predispose to myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms.
Germline GATA2 predisposes to myeloid neoplasms in the setting of a constitutional disorder affecting multiple organ systems.

Germline SAMD9L predisposes to acquired monosomy 7/del(7q) and MDS.

AML with mutated TP53 is associated with very poor outcome and defines a distinctly aggressive category across de novo, post-MDS, and therapy-related presentations.
In-frame bZIP CEBPA mutations define a favorable-prognosis AML entity without requiring biallelic CEBPA mutation.
When TP53 mutation overlaps another AML genetic category, it is usually predictive of worse prognosis and should be reported with the other abnormality.
In AML classification, single-gene mutation or gene-fusion categories take precedence over myelodysplasia-related gene-mutation and myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic categories.
Pure erythroid leukemia is typically TP53-mutated and is classified within AML with TP53 mutation in the ICC.
The remaining AML categories retain a blast requirement of at least 20%.

BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL is divided into lymphoid-only and multilineage BCR::ABL1-positive subsets.

In BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL, FISH detection of the translocation in granulocytes supports multilineage involvement, whereas FISH positivity confined to lymphoblasts supports lymphoid-only involvement.

After treatment of BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL, high RT-PCR positivity for BCR::ABL1 can persist despite little or no MRD by flow cytometry and other molecular MRD methods, which can affect MRD interpretation.
BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL with ABL-class fusions is important to recognize because these cases show a distinctive response pattern to ABL1-class tyrosine-kinase inhibitors.
CRLF2 rearrangement in BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL can often be detected by FISH or screened by CRLF2 flow cytometry because CRLF2 is upregulated.
B-ALL with MYC rearrangement is classified as an immature B-ALL entity distinct from aggressive mature B-cell lymphomas with MYC rearrangement.
B-ALL with MYC rearrangement has poor prognosis in the ICC summary table.
DUX4-rearranged B-ALL has excellent prognosis in children and adults, even with adverse features such as IKZF1 deletion.
FISH detection of DUX4 rearrangement is difficult.
DUX4 overexpression is specific for DUX4-rearranged B-ALL and can be detected by quantitative gene-expression testing or immunohistochemistry.
CD371 expression is associated with DUX4-rearranged B-ALL and may be identified by flow cytometry.
MEF2D-rearranged B-ALL has poor prognosis.
MEF2D-rearranged B-ALL can be assessed by whole-transcriptome sequencing or MEF2D FISH.
MEF2D-rearranged B-ALL with the common BCL9 fusion partner can be detected with available fusion FISH probes.
ZNF384-rearranged leukemia is a distinct rearrangement-defined entity that may present as B-ALL or B/myeloid MPAL.
ZNF362-rearranged cases with the same characteristic expression profile are grouped with ZNF384/ZNF362-rearranged B-ALL.
In ZNF384-rearranged B-ALL, prognosis varies by fusion partner, with EP300 associated with the best prognosis and TCF3 with the worst.
ZNF384/ZNF362-rearranged B-ALL can be assessed by whole-transcriptome sequencing, with FISH possible for some rearrangements.
NUTM1-rearranged B-ALL has favorable prognosis and, in infants, a much more favorable prognosis than KMT2A-rearranged leukemia.
NUTM1-rearranged B-ALL can be diagnosed with a standard NUTM1 break-apart FISH probe set.
HLF-rearranged B-ALL has very poor prognosis.
Anti-CD19 therapy and transplant have shown some promise in HLF-rearranged B-ALL.
CDX2/UBTF B-ALL is defined by concomitant FLT3/PAN3-region enhancer retargeting with CDX2 deregulation and a UBTF-region lesion producing UBTF::ATXN7L3.
CDX2/UBTF B-ALL appears to have poor outcome with conventional chemotherapy.
CDX2/UBTF B-ALL can be assessed using RT-PCR or whole-transcriptome sequencing for its defining lesions.
B-ALL with IKZF1 N159Y is recognized as a distinct point-mutation-defined entity.
The defining IKZF1 N159Y mutation in B-ALL can be detected by exome or gene-panel sequencing.
B-ALL with IKZF1 N159Y is assigned intermediate prognosis in the ICC summary table.
PAX5 P80R B-ALL has relatively favorable prognosis in the source discussion.
The PAX5 P80R B-ALL entity depends on biallelic PAX5 alteration through deletion or inactivation of the second allele.
The defining PAX5 P80R mutation in B-ALL can be detected by exome or gene-panel sequencing.
B-ALL with PAX5 P80R is summarized as intermediate prognosis overall and good prognosis in adults in the ICC summary table.
Pediatric ETV6::RUNX1-like B-ALL appears to have the same favorable prognosis as ETV6::RUNX1 B-ALL.
PAX5-altered B-ALL is a provisional subtype characterized by diverse PAX5 rearrangements, point mutations, and intragenic lesions.
Complete definition of PAX5-altered B-ALL requires gene-expression profiling.
B-ALL cases clustering with ZEB2 H1038R or IGH::CEBPE have poor prognosis.
ZEB2 H1038R and IGH::CEBPE lesions do not uniquely define the expression-defined provisional B-ALL group.

ETV6::RUNX1 defines an ICC B-ALL subtype with recurrent genetic abnormality.

cards.interpretation: In acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), recurrent RARA rearrangements involving IRF2BP2, NPM1, ZBTB16, STAT5B, STAT3, TBL1XR1, FIP1L1, or BCOR should be reported as the specific RARA-rearranged entity; as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities, they apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), recurrent KMT2A rearrangements with AFF1, AFDN, MLLT10, TET1, ELL, or MLLT1 should be reported as the specific KMT2A-rearranged entity; as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities, they apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), recurrent MECOM rearrangements involving MYC, ETV6, RUNX1, or the listed t(2;3) MECOM rearrangement should be reported as the specific MECOM-rearranged entity; as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities, they apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the rare recurring rearrangements involving PRDM16::RPN1, RBM15::MRTFA, NPM1::MLF1, NUP98::NSD1, ETV6::MNX1, KAT6A::CREBBP, PICALM::MLLT10, NUP98::KMD5A or other NUP98 partners, FUS::ERG, RUNX1::CBFA2T3, and CBFA2T3::GLIS2 are AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities and apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In the absence of an overriding AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality, a pathogenic somatic TP53 mutation with VAF at least 10%, with or without loss of the wild-type TP53 allele, defines the TP53-mutated category; cases are MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts and AML at at least 20% blasts.

In acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, for MPAL, B-lineage is assigned by strong CD19 plus at least 1 strongly expressed cytoplasmic CD79a, cCD22, or CD10, or by weak CD19 plus at least 2 of those markers strongly expressed.
Myeloblasts, monoblasts, and megakaryoblasts are included in the marrow or blood blast count used for AML classification.
In AML with monocytic or myelomonocytic differentiation, monoblasts and promonocytes are counted as blast equivalents, whereas abnormal monocytes are not.
In AML with PML::RARA or a variant RARA rearrangement, promyelocytes are counted as blast equivalents for classification.
Cases with a history of CML and at least 20% blasts are classified as CML in myeloid blast phase rather than AML with BCR::ABL1.
Remaining cases without a higher-priority AML-defining category are designated MDS/AML otherwise not specified when marrow or blood blasts are 10%-19%.

In-frame mutations affecting the CEBPA bZIP region confer favorable outcome in AML irrespective of whether they are monoallelic or biallelic and are assigned to the favorable ELN risk group. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

cards.interpretation: In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), RUNX1::RUNX1T1 and CBFB::MYH11 core-binding-factor AML are classified as favorable risk in the 2022 ELN genetic risk system; this risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

NPM1-mutated AML without FLT3-ITD is in the favorable ELN risk category when adverse-risk cytogenetic abnormalities are absent. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

NPM1-mutated AML with FLT3-ITD is intermediate risk in the 2022 ELN system irrespective of the FLT3-ITD allelic ratio, unless adverse-risk genetic lesions apply. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

Wild-type NPM1 AML with FLT3-ITD and no adverse-risk genetic lesions is intermediate risk irrespective of the FLT3-ITD allelic ratio. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

AML with t(9;11)(p21.3;q23.3)/MLLT3::KMT2A is intermediate risk, and this abnormality takes precedence over rare concurrent adverse-risk gene mutations. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), DEK::NUP214, BCR::ABL1, and KAT6A::CREBBP rearrangements are in the adverse 2022 ELN genetic risk category; this risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

KMT2A-rearranged AML other than t(9;11)/MLLT3::KMT2A is adverse risk; KMT2A partial tandem duplication is excluded from this adverse-risk entry. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), MECOM-rearranged disease, including inv(3)/t(3;3) involving GATA2 and MECOM and other t(3q26.2;v) MECOM rearrangements, is classified as adverse risk; the 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

TP53 mutation with VAF at least 10%, irrespective of monoallelic or biallelic status, is an adverse ELN genetic risk marker in AML. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), mutations in IDH1, IDH2, or DNMT3A are not assigned to a distinct 2022 ELN prognostic group on current evidence; the ELN risk system was developed mainly from intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

For NPM1-mutated AML, ELN risk assignment can change during therapy according to MRD response, including reclassification between favorable and intermediate risk based on MRD status. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), molecular MRD for NPM1, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, or CBFB::MYH11 that remains below 2% at the end of consolidation is associated with a very low relapse rate and is not prognostic of relapse at that level; it is operationally considered MRD negative.
Among responders with relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML treated with ivosidenib, molecular clearance was associated with longer remission duration and prolonged survival.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the FLT3-ITD allelic ratio is no longer used in the 2022 ELN risk classification; FLT3-ITD without adverse-risk genetic lesions is intermediate risk irrespective of allelic ratio. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.
In CEBPA-mutated AML, the paper reports longer leukemia survival for patients with a germline CEBPA mutation than for patients with two acquired CEBPA mutations.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11, concurrent KIT and/or FLT3 mutation does not alter the favorable ELN risk categorization; the 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

NPM1-mutated AML with adverse-risk cytogenetic abnormalities is categorized as adverse risk and has poor outcome. The 2022 ELN risk system is based mainly on intensively treated patients and may require modification for less-intensive therapy.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the emerging use of targeted inhibitors may affect prognostic outcomes in IDH1- or IDH2-mutated disease, so prognosis based on historical data may change with targeted therapy.

cards.interpretation: Best supportive care, including hydroxyurea, is an option for AML patients who cannot tolerate any antileukemic therapy or do not wish treatment.

CPX-351 is a treatment option for therapy-related AML or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes; in newly diagnosed patients aged 60-75 with secondary-type disease features it improved response and overall survival versus 7+3. Randomized data are lacking below age 60 and after prior MPN, and no benefit over 7+3 was shown for antecedent MDS with prior hypomethylating-agent exposure.

Oral azacitidine is approved as continued postremission treatment for AML in first CR/CRi after intensive induction when patients cannot complete intensive curative therapy including allogeneic HCT. Supporting data are lacking for patients younger than 55, CBF-AML, and use after GO- or CPX-351-based induction/consolidation; few trial patients had adverse-risk cytogenetics.
For FLT3-mutated AML treated intensively, midostaurin should be incorporated into first-line induction and consolidation therapy.
In patients aged 18-59 with FLT3-mutated AML, adding midostaurin to daunorubicin/cytarabine induction and high-dose cytarabine consolidation improved 4-year overall survival from 44.3% to 51.4%.

In FLT3-ITD-positive AML aged 18-75, preliminary meeting-abstract results from a phase 3 trial reported prolonged overall survival with quizartinib added to intensive induction/consolidation followed by maintenance versus placebo; peer-reviewed results were not yet available.
Gemtuzumab ozogamicin dosed with daunorubicin and cytarabine is approved for previously untreated CD33-positive AML.
In NPM1-mutated AML, adding gemtuzumab ozogamicin reduced relapse probability and increased mutant NPM1 molecular clearance but did not improve event-free survival.
For newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML not treated intensively, ivosidenib plus azacitidine improved EFS, CR/CRh, and median overall survival versus azacitidine plus placebo.

For relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML, ivosidenib salvage is a treatment option with single-agent CR rates around 20% and overall response including hematologic improvement around 40%.

For relapsed/refractory IDH2-mutated AML, enasidenib has clinically useful single-agent activity, although a randomized late-line study in patients at least 60 years did not improve overall survival versus conventional care.
After allogeneic HCT for FLT3-mutated AML, randomized studies show sorafenib maintenance reduces relapse risk, making a FLT3 inhibitor a reasonable posttransplant maintenance option.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), related donors carrying deleterious germline RUNX1 or CEBPA variants should not be used as stem-cell donors for allogeneic transplantation.
Because germline CEBPA predisposition remains after chemotherapy and can lead to independent AML, some experts advocate allogeneic HCT in first remission for affected patients.
Magrolimab has shown preliminary activity with azacitidine in newly diagnosed AML/MDS including TP53-mutated disease, but CD47-SIRP-alpha inhibitors remained in early clinical evaluation.
In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), menin inhibitors are under clinical evaluation for KMT2A-rearranged or NPM1-mutated disease rather than being established standard therapy.

In IDH1-mutated AML treated with ivosidenib, differentiation syndrome can occur; recommended management includes dexamethasone, hydroxyurea for co-occurring leukocytosis, and dose interruption or reduction.

In IDH2-mutated AML treated with enasidenib, differentiation syndrome can occur; recommended management includes dexamethasone, hydroxyurea for co-occurring leukocytosis, and dose interruption or reduction.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), fLT3 mutation testing should assess both ITD and TKD mutations; because longer FLT3-ITDs may be missed by NGS, continued capillary-electrophoresis testing is recommended.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), screening for PML::RARA, CBFB::MYH11, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, KMT2A rearrangements, and BCR::ABL1 is recommended when rapid information is needed for suitable therapy, chromosome morphology is poor, or typical morphology is present without the suspected cytogenetic abnormality.

For the listed AML RT-qPCR molecular targets—ABL1, BCR, CBFB, DEK, KMT2A, MLLT3, MYH11, NPM1, NUP214, RUNX1, RUNX1T1, and WT1—MRD positivity is defined as cycle threshold below 40 and negativity as cycle threshold at least 40 in at least 2 of 3 replicates.

cards.interpretation: Germline 5-prime CEBPA mutations have penetrance close to 100%, whereas germline 3-prime CEBPA mutations have lower penetrance; this distinction is clinically relevant to inherited CEBPA predisposition.
In germline RUNX1 predisposition, about 30% of patients have clonal hematopoiesis before leukemia development, with BCOR mutations predominating in that clonal hematopoiesis.
Among the RUNX1, ANKRD26, and ETV6 platelet-disorder predisposition syndromes, germline ANKRD26 mutation carriers generally have the lowest platelet counts.
Germline ETV6 mutations predispose to B-cell ALL and myeloid malignancies.
Germline RUNX1 mutations predispose to myeloid malignancies, T-cell ALL, and B-cell malignancies.
Germline ANKRD26 mutations have been associated only with myeloid malignancies to date.
When leukemia develops in germline RUNX1 predisposition, somatic mutation of the wild-type RUNX1 allele is common, together with acquired mutations in ASXL1, FLT3, GATA2, PHF6, SRSF2, and WT1.
For DDX41 germline predisposition, the DDX41 R525H hotspot occurs commonly in myeloid malignancies as a somatic mutation.
In germline CEBPA predisposition, second-allele CEBPA mutations are common and typically occur at the 3-prime end.

cards.interpretation: In patients investigated for unexplained cytopenia, finding two or more somatic mutations in the studied 40-gene panel was strongly predictive of the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML), with positive predictive value 0.88 (95% CI 0.84-0.92). These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.

cards.interpretation: For mutations measured in isolated peripheral-blood granulocytes, a VAF around 0.10 was associated with the best classification of the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML); the paper cautions that the applicable allele-burden threshold may vary when a different blood-cell source is used. These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.

In unexplained cytopenia, mutations in SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, JAK2, or RUNX1 had the highest predictive values for the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML), with positive predictive values of 0.88-0.97 irrespective of co-occurring mutations. These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.
